projects.title: Ribbon IK Plugin
projects.summary: A Maya plugin that builds ribbon IK setups from a selected joint chain, replacing an error-prone manual process with a parameterised dialog.

meta.Context: Built during Advanced Pipeline Topics, Carnegie Mellon ETC

sections.heading: The problem
body: Ribbon IK gives a limb or a tail smooth, volume-preserving deformation, but building one by hand is a long sequence of steps that has to be repeated identically for every chain: lofting the surface, generating follicles, creating and constraining controls, then wiring the blendshape options. Doing it twelve times for one creature is where mistakes get in.
I wrote the plugin so the setup becomes a single parameterised operation, and so the result is identical every time.

sections.heading: What it does
list: Builds a ribbon surface and control rig from a selected root joint, with configurable controller count and ribbon width.
Handles joint pointing direction and normal flipping, which are the two settings that most often need correcting per-chain.
Optionally generates the curve needed for spline IK, and the control hierarchy, as independent toggles.
Exposes blendshape options — up/down and left/right sine waves, and reel — for secondary motion without hand-animating each control.

sections.heading: Notes
body: The interface is deliberately plain. Technical artists reach for a tool mid-task, so every option is visible at once rather than nested behind tabs, and the defaults produce a usable rig without changing anything.
I later taught a session on authoring tools like this one in Maya with Python and MEL for the Advanced 3D Pipeline course at the ETC.

figures.caption: The build dialog. Controller count, ribbon width and joint pointing direction cover the settings that change most often between chains.

projects.title: Penguin Action Toolkit
projects.summary: An accessible, extensible action-game framework for Unity, released free on the Unity Asset Store. I built the node-based editor and contributed to the animation and behaviour architecture.

meta.Team: Six-person team at Carnegie Mellon ETC, advised by Dave Culyba and Tom Corbett

sections.heading: Overview
body: Action games have a deep, well-understood structure — move sets, actions, modifiers, cancel windows — but Unity gives you no scaffolding for any of it. Small teams end up rebuilding the same state handling from scratch and running out of time before the game feels good.

Penguin Action Toolkit provides that scaffolding, along with documentation, tutorials and sample content, so a designer can iterate on combat feel instead of on plumbing. The framework is built to stay structured yet flexible, for developers who want to code rather than avoid it — every system is meant to be extended, not just configured.

sections.heading: Core systems
body: Character Locomotion handles movement — player input, character movement and camera behaviour — through modular motor and animator components that can be swapped independently.

Character Abilities are triggered containers called Action States, defined by State Modifiers that control animations, effects, sounds and locomotion changes, so a designer builds a move by composing modifiers rather than writing a new state machine.

figures.caption: The toolkit's editor surfaces: the PAT_Toolkit menu, the MoveSet / Action / Modifier hierarchy, and the character inspector that ties them to a runtime node graph.

sections.heading: Node graph editor
body: The GUI Node Graph Editor lets a designer build a character's action structure by adding nodes and dragging in scripts, instead of hand-wiring state machines in code. Character, move set, action and modifier nodes are colour-coded so the shape of a behaviour tree is legible at a glance.

figures.caption: An Action State's component stack — attack, locomotion, tag and montage-speed modifiers stacked on a single node.

embeds.title: Node Graph System — Penguin Action Toolkit

sections.heading: My contribution
list: Designed and built the node-based GUI editor, modelled on the Unreal Engine Blueprint system, so that designers can author and read character behaviour visually.
Contributed to the architecture connecting character nodes, move sets, actions and modifiers.
Created character rigs and animations for the sample content shipped with the package.

sections.heading: Release
body: The toolkit is published free on the Unity Asset Store for Unity 2022.3 and URP. The team ran a workshop and a game jam around it to test whether developers outside the project could pick it up from the documentation alone.

figures.caption: The node editor. Character, move set, action and modifier nodes are colour-coded so the shape of a behaviour tree is legible at a glance.

projects.title: Quadruped Rigging Toolset
projects.summary: A toolset for building quadruped rigs, reducing repeated manual setup across animals that share a skeletal structure but differ in proportion.

sections.heading: Overview
body: Quadrupeds share a common skeletal logic but vary enormously in proportion, and rebuilding the same spine, limb and foot systems per animal is slow. The toolset generalises the parts that stay constant so that what remains is the per-animal judgement.

The workflow has two steps. First, the tool creates a guide that is placed to match the animal's proportions. Then a single build operation generates the rig from that guide, so the only per-animal work is fitting the guide and adjusting a handful of options.

sections.heading: What it builds
list: A spine with a configurable number of controllers, so a long-backed animal and a compact one can each get the density of control they need.
A tail with its own controller count, plus optional blendshape-driven secondary motion — up/down and left/right sine waves, and reel — so the tail can move without hand-animating every control.
Front limbs, rear limbs, head and tail, each set up to follow the part of the body they hang from.

sections.heading: The following system
body: Most of what makes a quadruped read as a single animal is how the parts inherit motion from each other. The toolset exposes this as four independent toggles: front limbs follow the spine, rear limbs follow the hip, the head follows the neck, and the tail follows the hip.

Keeping these as options rather than fixed behaviour means the same tool covers an animal whose head should be driven by the neck and one whose head needs to stay independent, without a separate rig template for each.

sections.heading: Notes
body: As with my Ribbon IK Plugin, the interface is a single plain panel with every option visible at once, and the defaults produce a usable rig without changing anything. The build can also be run in stages rather than all at once, so a rig can be regenerated after adjusting the guide without redoing the parts that were already right.

figures.caption: The build panel. Guide creation, spine and tail controller counts, the following-system toggles and the build mode are all on one screen.

projects.title: Character Rigs
projects.summary: A selection of biped rigs — stylised and realistic, for game and film pipelines — built with full FK/IK switching, space switching and animator-facing control layouts.

sections.heading: Overview
body: These rigs share one priority: the animator should never have to think about the rig. Controls sit where the hand goes, FK/IK switching is seamless, and naming is consistent enough that tools can be written against it.

Below are four characters from that body of work: an assassin, a stylised girl with a separate facial rig, an alien, and a swordsman. Each is shown in motion so the rig can be judged by how it behaves, not by how it looks in a screenshot.

sections.heading: Assassin
body: A complete character rig, finished in one month using the mGear framework. I built a dynamic cloth system driven by RBF and corrective blendshapes, and came away with a working command of mGear and of a complex rigging pipeline. To test the rig I modified a motion-capture animation and applied it to the character. The clips show the finished rig and a closer look at its details.

sections.heading: Stylised girl
body: A stylised biped, shown with a body rig demo and, separately, the face rig, so the facial controls can be judged on their own rather than lost inside a full-body shot.

sections.heading: Alien
body: A practice rig built by following AntCGI's tutorial. Working through it taught me how to set up IK stretch and shrink and a complex space-swap system, and made me much more comfortable with Maya's Node Editor and attribute setup.

sections.heading: Swordman
body: For this character I implemented weapon attachment, facial controls, and low-cost cloth and hair controls suited to mobile platforms.

projects.title: Creature Rigs
projects.summary: Non-biped setups — a kraken, an eagle and a Chinese dragon — where the deformation problem changes with every anatomy.

sections.heading: Overview
body: Creature work is where generic rigging solutions stop being enough. A kraken needs many tentacles that all move as continuous, flexible curves; a wing needs a skeleton that folds and spreads like the real thing; a dragon needs a long spine that reads as one continuous motion.

sections.heading: Kraken
body: I used the ribbon IK method to procedurally generate the rig for every tentacle, and that work eventually became the Ribbon IK Plugin.

sections.heading: Eagle
body: Built for a semester-long school project. It got me familiar with animal rigs, especially how bird wings work and how to achieve that behaviour with a skeleton.

projects.title: AI MetaHuman Pipeline
projects.summary: A pipeline that takes an AI-generated base mesh through ZBrush sculpting, topology-preserving transfer in Maya and XGen grooming into a rigged, animation-ready UE5 MetaHuman.

meta.Tools: Maya, ZBrush, Mari, Substance Painter, Unreal Engine 5

sections.heading: Overview
body: Building a production-quality digital human from scratch is slow, and most of the time goes into modelling, rigging and skinning before a character can be tested at all. This pipeline explores how AI-generated geometry can shorten that path without giving up control over the result.

The key constraint is topology. The AI stage produces a base mesh that already follows MetaHuman topology, so once the mesh has been sculpted it can be transferred onto the MetaHuman preset model, which lets the new character inherit the existing rig and skin data instead of being rebuilt. Everything after the AI stage is artist-directed.

sections.heading: 1. Reference
body: Gather the reference imagery that defines the character's design, proportions and facial features, taken from a range of angles and expressions.

figures.caption: Reference images collected for the character, covering front, three-quarter and profile views.

sections.heading: 2. Base mesh
body: Generate a base mesh with Hyper3D that already follows MetaHuman topology. This is what makes the rest of the pipeline possible.

figures.caption: Base mesh generated by Hyper3D with MetaHuman topology.

sections.heading: 3. Sculpting
body: Refine the mesh in ZBrush, adding detail and correcting the likeness while keeping the original topology intact.

figures.caption: The mesh after detailed sculpting in ZBrush, with the original topology preserved. Front view.
Three-quarter view of the same sculpt. The edge flow around the eyes, nose and mouth is unchanged from the base mesh.

sections.heading: 4. Transfer
body: Import the sculpted mesh into Maya and transfer its vertex data onto the MetaHuman preset model. The preset keeps its rig and skin data, so the new character inherits them without re-rigging or re-skinning. Export the result as MetaHuman DNA for Unreal Engine 5.

figures.caption: The sculpted head on the MetaHuman preset in Maya, inheriting its body rig and facial control panel.

sections.heading: 5. Hair groom
body: Author groom guides in Maya with XGen to generate the hair, brows and beard.

figures.caption: Groom guides for the hair, eyebrows and beard, authored in Maya with XGen.
Hair generated from the guides, with the guides still displayed over the result.

sections.heading: 6. Body assembly
body: Repeat the same process for the body, connect it to the head, and export the MetaHuman DNA into UE5 using the plugin.

sections.heading: Where the artist stays in control
body: The AI step only supplies a starting point. Judgement stays with the artist at every stage after it: sculpting for likeness and character, checking the transfer, and directing the groom. The AI contributes speed to a first mesh, and MetaHuman-compatible topology means the expensive rigging and skinning work is inherited rather than repeated.

sections.heading: Final result
body: The finished character in Unreal Engine 5, rendered under different lighting and framing.

figures.caption: Low-key portrait lighting, showing the groomed hair and beard on the finished character.
Close-up of the same setup, showing skin detail, brows and the beard groom.
Front view with neutral studio lighting.
Full-body A-pose with the assembled body, clothing and hair.

sections.heading: Facial capture test
body: As a final test of the result, the finished character was driven with facial capture.

projects.title: Project Good Boy
projects.summary: A character-driven puzzle game in Unreal Engine 5. I handle art assets, character modelling, rigging, animation and gameplay programming.

sections.heading: Overview
body: Good Boy (working title) is a puzzle-solving dog simulator. You wake as a dog in a streamer's bedroom with human intent and animal tools — no hands, only paws, weight, teeth and bark — and the only way out is to solve the room before she notices. Every locked drawer and high shelf becomes a problem of physics and timing, and the streamer who owns the room is both the obstacle and the clock.

The game runs on a repeating daily cycle: free exploration in the morning, supervision before the broadcast, real risk while she is live, then consequences and a reset at night. Hidden values track suspicion, affection and dream stability, and pushing too far ejects you from the loop.
It is a solo project, so it covers the whole path from modelling, rigging and animation through to gameplay code in C++ and Blueprint.

sections.heading: The dog controller
body: The central technical problem is that a long-bodied quadruped does not fit Unreal's upright, capsule-based character model. The controller is a bespoke C++ layer over Character Movement, built around that mismatch.

Locomotion is driven by Motion Matching rather than a hand-built state machine. Control Rig foot IK with per-foot locking removes the sliding that Motion Matching leaves during low-speed turns, and lets the front and rear feet find the floor independently on slopes and steps. Because secondary collision volumes do not push the root capsule, head clipping is handled with predictive sweeps before each move.

sections.heading: Production timeline
body: Development is documented in a 36-week log, grouped into eleven phases. The target is a ten-minute vertical slice: one room, one heroine, a handful of polished dog interactions and a single complete loop that ends on a narrative beat.
list: Weeks 1–3 · Nov — Finding the Dog. Settled the core fantasy, the single-room setting and the dog's limited set of verbs.
Weeks 4–6 · Nov–Dec — Building the Body. First contact with Unreal: the bespoke controller on Character Movement, and the decision to commit to Motion Matching.
Weeks 7–9 · Dec–Jan — The Room as a Puzzle Box. Narrowed the scope to a short bedroom experience, defined the streamer's daily schedule and drafted the system architecture.
Weeks 10–13 · Jan — Making the Dog Move. Motion Matching locomotion, rotation and camera behaviour, jump and fall logic, and the five-phase dream loop.
Weeks 14–17 · Feb — Bringing the World to Life. Idle variety, a NavMesh-driven heroine, grooms, in-room screens and ambient animation.
Weeks 19–21 · Mar — Polish and Structure. Custom camera collision, the limits of capsule collision, and a single diagram of the whole architecture.
Weeks 22–25 · Mar–Apr — Learning from Other Animals. Research into horse controllers and animal collision that fed back into the dog, and the decision to target a ten-minute slice.
Weeks 28–29 · May — Shaping the Demo. Consolidated the game's identity and defined the flow of the slice.
Week 30 · May — Interaction and Event Triggers. An interface-based interaction framework and overlap triggers that turn the room into a solvable puzzle.
Weeks 31–33 · Jun — Wiring the Loop. The heroine's perception and suspicion system, the first complete puzzle, and the full day-phase loop with night reset.
Weeks 34–36 · Jun–Jul — First Playable. Assembled the slice end to end, added foot locking and camera polish, and ran the first structured playtest.

sections.heading: Current status
body: The slice is playable start to finish and runs nine to twelve minutes. In the first playtest, testers understood being a dog immediately and reacted well to the moment of slipping past the heroine while she is distracted. The main finding is that suspicion needs a readable in-world signal, so being caught does not feel arbitrary, and that is the next design problem.

projects.title: Kraken Unleashed
projects.summary: A three-month team PBR animation production in Unreal Engine 5, entered in The Rookies Award 2024. I handled rigging, animation, directing, VFX, post-process and the environment.

meta.Context: Advanced Pipeline Topics, Carnegie Mellon ETC

sections.heading: Overview
body: The kraken's tentacles are the whole problem. Eight long, tapering limbs need to deform smoothly along their length, curl convincingly at the tip, and stay art-directable rather than simulated — an animator has to be able to pose them.
I built the rig around ribbon IK. Doing that setup by hand for every tentacle showed how much of it was repetitive, and after the project I turned the process into the Ribbon IK Plugin.
The project was a team production finished in three months and entered in The Rookies Award 2024.

sections.heading: Contribution
list: Rigging: built and iterated the full creature rig through production.
Animation and directing: animated the creature and directed the piece.
VFX, post-process and the environment, all in Unreal Engine 5.

sections.heading: What I took from it
body: The project gave me hands-on experience with complex model rigging, and with cutting repetitive work by replacing manual steps with procedural solutions. The tentacle rig is where that approach started, and it is the origin of my Ribbon IK plugin for Maya.

projects.title: Silt Symphony
projects.summary: A digital installation shown in the Spring Undergraduate Exhibition at SAIC Galleries, Chicago.

meta.Venue: SAIC Galleries, 33 E. Washington St., Chicago
meta.Tools: Unreal Engine 5, Maya, Substance Painter, Substance Designer

sections.heading: About the work
body: Silt Symphony is a digital installation made for my BFA show. It is built from a single dynamic 3D environment, presented as three perspectives of the same space. I made it over about two months for PC, using Unreal Engine 5, Maya and Substance Painter and Designer, and it was shown in the Spring Undergraduate Exhibition at SAIC Galleries in Chicago.

sections.heading: Concept
body: The work is made of objects that are inseparable from my growing up in Baoshan, Shanghai, an industrial town built around one of the largest steel factories in China. Through animation, and a poem that I wrote and read in my hometown dialect, I made a memorial for a hometown I love and that is gradually disappearing. It was once full of factories, construction sites, waste gas, smog and countless blue-collar workers.
The piece carries a strange nostalgia: that of a kid who belonged to an industrial world he can never return to in the age of deindustrialisation.
